answer: LINE changes the training objective by sampling edges in proportion to their weights and then using a weighted loss for each sampled edge, so an edge with weight w contributes w times the gradient of the base loss rather than being duplicated w times in the data. In practice, this is done by optimizing a weighted negative-sampling objective such as -w[log σ(u·v) + k E_{n~P_n} log σ(-u·n)], where the edge weight multiplies the whole per-edge loss. Because the weight appears as a scalar multiplier on the gradient of a single sampled edge, it preserves the relative importance of heavy edges without making the optimization unstable through repeated identical updates or excessively large step counts from literal edge replication.
